Landscape Architecture Landscape architecture is a 126-credit curriculum leading to the Bachelor of Landscape Architecture (B.L.A.) degree.
Accredited by the Landscape Architecture Accreditation Board of the ASLA, the curriculum is designed to prepare undergraduates for professional careers in public and private practice.
Landscape architecture is a profession that involves the design, planning, preservation, and restoration of the landscape by applying art, science, and technology to achieve the best use of our land and water resources.
Landscape architects design and plan parks, plazas, and recreation areas; residential, institutional and commercial developments; transportation facilities, new towns and campus landscapes, and green infrastructure.
They are also involved in planning and designing landscapes in coastal and inland developments impacted by climate.
The requirements of this curriculum include preparation in the basic arts and sciences.

The major includes 63-64 credits of professional core classes (LAR 101, 201, 202, 243, 244, 300, 301, 302, 343, 344, 345, 346, 353, 354, 443, 444, 445, 447, 450); 28-29 credits of supporting requirements (ART 207; GEG 101; PLS 150; CHM 100, 101 or 103 or PHY 109, or GEO 100, or 103; CPL 410, CPL 434, 538; MTH 111103; and PLS 200); and 7-8 credits of supporting electives.
Students will also take general education classes and 6-7 credits of free electives.
Students accepted into landscape architecture are required to maintain a grade point average of at least 2.50 with no landscape architecture grades below a letter C.
Students failing to maintain this minimum may be removed from the program and required to reapply once this requirement is satisfied.
Students are required to own a P.C. laptop computer by the time they enter the program.
Specifications are available from the Landscape Architecture Program Office or from the URI Bookstore (Ramtech).
URI's Landscape Architecture Program (LAR) is competitive.
Accreditation standards regarding staff and facilities limit the number of students accepted into the major to 20 per year.

While enrolled in the program, students will be reviewed twice during their course of studies: first for admission into the lower-division design sequence and again for acceptance into the upper- division B.L.A. major.
Admission into the lower-division design sequence courses (LAR 243 and 244) requires department approval.
Approximately 50 percent of the openings are filled by students who enter as incoming freshmen and who maintain a minimum 2.50 grade point average with no grades in LAR courses below a C.
The remaining openings are filled by matriculated students wishing to transfer into landscape architecture from other majors.

The Department of Mathematics’ name does not accurately and fully reflect the research work, course and degree offerings, and trajectory of the department.
A more representative name for the department is the Department of Mathematics and Applied Mathematical Sciences.
Furthermore, with national trends leaning towards applied math, it is imperative that students (current and prospective) and colleagues (at URI and outside of URI) are aware of our applied math research and programs.

This name change is expected to help us in recruiting students, developing research collaborations (both within and outside the institution), and attracting new hires in applied math.
According to the U.S.
Bureau of Labor of Statistics, “Employment in math occupations is projected to grow 27 percent from 2019 to 2029, much faster than the average for all occupations, and will add about 56,100 jobs.
Growth is anticipated as businesses and government agencies continue to emphasize the use of big data, which math occupations analyze.”1 Applied mathematics is very broadly defined as using mathematics to solve problems in a wide variety of fields of study.
The name applied mathematical sciences is more focused on applying mathematics to sciences, (including a recent trend in mathematical biology, a direction in which we intend to grow) and will include the department’s involvement in the fields of actuarial science (currently done as a double major with finance) and our growing work in data science.
The department officially voted to change the department name to Department of Mathematics and Applied Mathematical Sciences on September 14, 2020. 1 https://www.bls.gov/ooh/math/home.htm

Degree Offerings.
The department has two track options at all levels, B.S. general and applied math option, M.S. pure and applied math track, and Ph.D. pure and applied math track.
The applied math tracks, at both the B.S. and Ph.D. level, have been offered for decades.
The B.S. applied math option is selected by the majority (over 67%) of B.S. math majors.
Because of this track’s popularity, in 2018 the faculty broadened the applied track offering at the M.S. level and also created the accelerated five-year B.S. – M.S. program in applied math.
Currently, more than half of our M.S. and Ph.D. graduate-level students are in the applied math track.
Additionally, the department is now in the process of creating a one-year graduate certificate in Applied Mathematics and exploring a Biomathematics minor.
With the College of Business, the department developed a curriculum outline that leads to a double major in finance and applied math (unofficially called pre-actuarial science track).
This curriculum prepares students for the first actuarial exam and provides a foundation for successful employment as an actuary.

When funding was available, the department also brought students on well-received day trips to PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC) in New York.
In fact, one of our recent applied math graduates, Lauren Black, has taken a position as an associate actuary at PWC directly after graduation.
A senior manager at PwC, Larry Rubin was consulted with structuring our current curriculum.
According to the U.S.
Bureau of Labor of Statistics, “Employment of actuaries is projected to grow 18 percent from 2019 to 2029, much faster than the average for all occupations.”2 Currently there are 9 double finance and applied math majors and the department seeks to expand interest in the area of financial mathematics.
Course Offerings.
The department has always had two course codes, MTH and AMS (Applied Mathematical Sciences) and offers numerous applied math courses, e.g.
MTH 441 Introduction to Partial Differential Equations, MTH 418/518 Matrix Analysis, MTH 471/571 Numerical Analysis, MTH 472 Numerical Linear Algebra, MTH 481/581 Optimization Methods, MTH 572 Numerical Partial Differential Equations, AMS 490 Intermediate Topics in Applied Mathematics, and AMS 590 Advanced Topics in Applied Mathematics.

We also plan to propose, with the AMS course code, the following courses: AMS 210 Introduction to Mathematics Biology, AMS 310 Mathematical Modeling, AMS 410 Mathematical Biology, AMS 528 Mathematical and Computational Analysis of Data, and AMS/DSP 393G Introduction to Predictive Analytics.
Research/Activities.
In addition to having some faculty members with earned doctorates in Applied Mathematics, our faculty conduct research in applied math topics.
Areas include, but are not limited to, Numerical Linear Algebra, Mathematical Biology and Modeling, Financial Mathematics, Applied Probability, Combinatorics, Graph Theory, Partial Differential Equations, and Difference Equations.
Below is a brief summary of some of the work being done by our faculty. - Development of a statistical/linear algebra method that is used for computing the Principal Component Analysis (PCA) for extremely large data sets.
Used in numerous applications (e.g. image processing, genomics, robotics).

It was featured as a chapter in the book Handbook of Big Data, a bases for svds.m in the commercial software MATLAB, and the R-package (irlba) has been downloaded over 2,500,000 times.3 2 https://www.bls.gov/ooh/math/actuaries.htm 3 https://ipub.com/dev-corner/apps/r-package-downloads/ (need to type in irlba under Packages – select cumulative) 2

- Development of probabilistic methods in different contexts: discrete structures as well as high- dimensional spaces.
Discrete random structures are essential in the design of algorithms and error correcting codes.
They are also used to model a large variety of objects in physics, biology, and network science.
Methods of high-dimensional probability play a central role in applications in dimension reduction in data science, signal processing, matrix completion, theoretical computer science. - Development of a new model for measuring connectedness in networks using local information that can be used in detecting artificially inflated importance in social networks. - Research in pursuit-evasion games on graphs provides theoretical underpinnings for real-life search and retrieval strategies - Research is being conducted on the statistical and econometric properties of the market microstructure (which happens every millisecond making this system hard to analyze).
Nowadays, trading is performed using an electronic double auction system where offers to buy are matched with offers to sell.

Most stock exchanges in the world are operating within this new framework and while every exchange has its own rules, many follow the same principles.
An array that stores and displays the information of the price and the quantity at which people are willing to buy or sell certain asset is called a Limit Order Book.
Understanding its statistical properties has become of critical importance to many financial institutions such as banks, hedge funds and independent market participants to improve the way they perform their trades: via algorithmic trading. - Research is done in developing a systematic understanding and numerical methods in relation to polynomial and rational eigenvalue problems.
These problems arise either directly or as approximations of more general nonlinear eigenvalue problems.

Some applications leading to nonlinear eigenvalue problems include vibrations of fluid-solid structures, structural dynamics, computational quantum chemistry, electromagnetic modeling of particle accelerators, and stability analysis of time-delay systems. - Classical mathematical models from population biology and epidemiology including the Leslie matrix model and the Lotka-Volterra predator prey and cooperation and competition models are based on difference or differential equations.
More recent models such as a model for the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) and different respiratory viruses such as H1N1 and Covid-19 are investigated using as principal tool difference or differential equations.
In fact, the basic reproductive number as major indicator of severity epidemics is derived from the stability analysis of the basic difference equation model of epidemics.
In addition, difference equations models are used in modeling some phenomena in population genetics, cell biology, and physiology as well.

After several rounds of discussions between the healthcare management program director (Sean Edmund Rogers) and URI Online leadership, as well as analysis of current and prospective student data, we wish to make the following changes to streamline URI’s healthcare management offerings and to enhance their marketability: 1. Ask #1: Offer a single healthcare management graduate certificate instead of the two separate certificates that currently exist, and allow a wider selection of healthcare management (MHM) courses to count towards that single certificate.

2.
Ask #2: Change the composition of the M.S. degree such that it straightforwardly requires the completion of 30 credits of MHM credits.
Currently, the M.S. degree is structured as the combination of (1) one 12-credit post-baccalaureate certificate, (2) a second post-bac certificate, (3) one MHM elective, and (4) a practicum capstone.
This totals 10 MHM classes and 30 MHM credits.
The certificate portion of this is a so-called stackable certificate approach, with 24 of the 30 credits coming from these two post-bac certificates.
Our desire is to streamline the M.S. in Healthcare Management degree such that it is comprised of 30 MHM credits whether or not a student completes a graduate certificate en passant.
Our primary objective with this entire change proposal is #1 above – to make earning a graduate certificate in healthcare management at URI more accessible.
Per URI Online recruiters and prospectors, there has not been a single expression of interest in the post- bac certificate in quality improvement.

Students are certainly interested in quality improvement and this is an important topic in healthcare; however, none have expressed a desire to devote an entire program of study to this subject.
Any interest in earning a healthcare grad certificate at URI has been directed toward the other existing certificate in health administration.
Additionally, prospective students have expressed strong interest in being able to earn a certificate by taking courses outside of the strict structure that currently exists (at present, three of the four courses in each certificate are prescribed).
The current structure limits when students can begin and complete a certificate – they must wait until the carousel of courses comes back around for them to hop on, and in some cases that can be a year-long wait.
Creating a single certificate in healthcare management enables URI to alleviate these pain points and reach a wider audience of prospective students.
We have found that most prospective students interested in a grad certificate wish to begin quickly, and URI Online has the structure in place to enable that to happen.
The limiting factor is our current program design.

A side effect of creating a single graduate certificate in healthcare management is that the “stackable certificate” design of the M.S. would need to go away and be replaced with a straightforward 30-credit MHM approach.
There is no evidence that removing the notion of stackable certificates would do harm.
No prospects in recent memory have expressed interest in earning the stackable certificates as a pathway to the M.S. degree.
In fact, it has created confusion during prospect calls and sessions. 2

As a final sidenote on the topic of stackable certificates, in my professional opinion (as a scholar of human resources) such a design may even adversely impact URI’s ability to provide accessible healthcare management graduate education to Rhode Islanders and beyond.
As I learned this summer via meetings with enrollment services, financial aid, and URI Online, our healthcare management graduate certificates do not qualify for federal financial aid.
Some graduate certificate programs around the country do qualify for federal aid, but our healthcare management ones were determined not to.
Thus, students must pay for all certificate credits (up to 24 under the current “stackable” model) with non- federal financial aid, such as out of pocket or via private loans.
At current rates, that amounts to $18,792 for two URI certificates.
This has led to more than one prospective student not applying or enrolling at URI this summer and fall.
The streamlining we propose potentially removes barriers to access and may help put URI graduate education within reach for more aspiring healthcare professionals and leaders.

Summary: In sum, the newly-proposed M.S. degree structure would include all the same courses as before.
We are not changing the curricular offering at all - we are simply proposing that the stackable certificate design be removed.
That’s ask #2 above.
And we are asking for it to be removed because we wish to offer a single grad certificate in healthcare management that offers flexibility and frequency for learners (instead of two separate certificates that are narrowly tailored).
That’s ask #1 above. 6.
